The facility includes a reference center with two large auditoriums, smaller classrooms, and a Medical Simulation Center designed for training medical professionals in performing procedures and laparoscopic surgeries. 2. Annually, over 15,000 physicians and other healthcare professionals receive training at this center. 3. The offices of the Department of Medical Education are also located within this facility. 4. The Biomedical Science Research Building, a six-story structure that opened in 2006, provides 472,000 gross square feet of research space dedicated to basic biomedical sciences. 5. This building houses 240 laboratory modules and 140 faculty offices, along with classrooms and a 300-seat auditorium situated in an elliptical facility in front of the main building. 6. The architectural design of the building has received several prestigious awards. 7. The building is home to the internationally renowned U-M Program for Neurology Research and Discovery (P-FUND), which recently received a $5 million donation from Alfred Taubman. 8. The U-M Neuropathy Center, one of only four centers in the nation recognized and funded by the Neuropathy Association, is also part of this program. 9. Research laboratories in the building are organized around themes such as nanotechnology, neuroscience, developmental biology, molecular imaging, molecular mechanisms of disease, immunology, geriatrics and biogerontology, regenerative medicine, and organogenesis. 10. The Life Science Institute (LSI), established in 2000 and completed in 2003 at a cost of $100 million, is a six-story facility with 230,000 square feet of wet bench, dry lab, and core facility research space. 11. LSI houses 25-30 faculty-led research teams spanning 16 different departments and schools, including the U-M Medical School. 12. The LSI is part of a three-building facility that includes Palmer Commons (99,000 square feet, containing a conference/meeting center and the Bioinformatics Program) and the Undergraduate Science Building (140,000 square feet, with classrooms and conference centers). 13. LSI core facilities include DNA sequencing, flow cytometry, functional genomics, metabolic phenotyping, and a state-of-the-art vivarium for small animals and fish. 14. The LSI has a partnership with the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. 15. The facility contains several world-renowned centers and programs, including the Center for Structural Genomics, the Center for Stem Cell Biology, the Center for Structural Biology, and the Michigan Bioinformatics Program. 16. The Medical Science I and II buildings, opened in 1958 and 1969 respectively, house the Medical School and UMHS administrative offices, research laboratories, and faculty offices. 17. Medical Science II serves as the primary facility for medical student education. 18. The Medical Science Research Buildings I, II, and III, opened in 1986, 1989, and 1995 respectively, provide basic research laboratories and shared core facilities for U-M biomedical researchers. 19. MSRB I houses the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) offices, as the University of Michigan is one of 12 HHMI sites in the country. 20. The Kresge Complex, built between 1954 and 1963, includes the Kresge Medical Research buildings and the Kresge Hearing Research Institute, which houses basic otolaryngology labs and other research facilities. 21. The Kresge Complex is also home to the Michigan Diabetes Research & Training Center, the Upjohn Center for Clinical Pharmacology, and the Michigan Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center, which recently received a $10 million grant. 22. According to the University of Michigan Health System Master Plan, the Kresge buildings are identified as sites for future development and are likely to be replaced with new research facilities in the coming years. 23. The North Ingalls Building, an 11-story structure purchased by the university in 1977, houses administrative offices for U-M Hospitals & Health Centers and various clinical departments. 24. The School of Public Health (SPH), established in 1941, is home to a top-rated clinical research program and has consistently ranked 1 in Health Management since 1993. 25. In 2007, SPH was ranked 5 among Public Health Schools in the U.S. News rankings. 26. In fall 2006, SPH completed construction on the Crossroads and Research Tower, a seven-story, 125,000-square-foot building housing 17 conference rooms and 133 laboratory benches. 27. SPH is one of two lead institutions in the Finland-United States Investigation of Non-Insulin-Dependent Diabetes Mellitus Genetics (FUSION) study group, which recently discovered four new genes causing Type II Diabetes. 28. SPH also houses the world-famous U-M Autism and Communication Disorders Center, a leading center in clinical treatment and genetics research for autism. 29. SPH has 180 faculty members across five academic departments: Biostatistics, Environmental Health Science, Epidemiology, Health Behavior and Health Education, and Health Management and Policy. 30. The East Ann Arbor Health and Geriatrics Center, opened in 1996 and renovated in 2006, provides outpatient clinics in general internal medicine, general pediatrics, obstetrics & gynecology, and primary and specialty care services of the Turner Geriatric Clinic. 31. The Turner Geriatric Clinic is consistently ranked among the top 10 geriatrics centers in the nation. 32. The East Ann Arbor facility also includes a pharmacy, a patient education center, a blood-draw station, and educational facilities. 33. An adjoining suite houses MRI, CT, and mammography imaging facilities. 34. Specialty clinics tailored to elderly care include the Foot Care Clinic, Incontinence Clinic, Mobility Enhancement Clinic, Cognitive Disorders Clinic, Movement Disorders Clinic, Deep Brain Stimulation Clinic, Geropsychiatry Clinic, Sexual Health Clinic, Transitional Care Clinic, and Women’s Health Clinic. 35. The Rachel Upjohn Depression Center, located near the Geriatrics Center, opened in 2006 and is the first Comprehensive Depression Center in the country. 36. The 112,500-square-foot facility houses 335 offices and outpatient treatment rooms, a 120-seat auditorium, and two telemedicine offices to assist patients in remote areas. 37. The center combines all outpatient psychiatric and substance abuse care for adults and children into one facility. 38. It contains leading centers for comprehensive treatment of depression and bipolar disorder and also houses a library and art gallery. 39. The facility includes space for research, education, and administrative programs of the U-M Depression Center. 40. The center is named after Rachel Mary (Upjohn) Meader, who, along with her husband Edwin, donated $10 million toward the building’s construction. 41. Additional facilities within the center include the Sleep Research Center, MRI Simulator, Brain Imaging Center, and Stress and Neuroendocrine Program. 42. The Med Sport Suite, located in Domino’s Farms, houses the Sports Medicine Division of Orthopedic Surgery, a 45,000-square-foot facility with 15 examination rooms and on-site radiology. 43. The Med Sport Suite was established by Gerald A. O’Connor, a professor of Orthopedic Surgery at U-M and a past president of the American Orthopaedic Society for Sports Medicine.
